segments.say: Think about the last time you read a good book. Not a menu or a message, but a story you sank into. When you read the words on the page, did you hear them? Was there a voice, reading along inside your head? Many people say yes, of course. Others pause, and say, actually, I'm not sure.

It's often said that reading is a kind of silent speech, that we all quietly say the words to ourselves as our eyes move along the line. It feels obvious to many readers. But as we saw with the beepers, what feels obvious about our own minds isn't always what's there when someone checks carefully.
Before we look at the science, here's a story that people have told about reading for a very long time.

show.title: An old story about silent reading

segments.say: In his Confessions, written around the year 400, Augustine of Hippo describes watching Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, reading. His eyes moved over the page and his heart searched out the meaning, Augustine writes, but his voice and tongue were at rest. Augustine seems to have found this worth remarking on, and for a long time the passage was taken as evidence that silent reading was rare in the ancient world.

show.what: Described his teacher Ambrose reading with his eyes only, his voice and tongue at rest

segments.say: Historians have since questioned that. In 1968, the classicist Bernard Knox published an article arguing that silent reading was not as unusual in antiquity as people had assumed, and others have added evidence since. So the story may tell us more about Augustine's curiosity than about how everyone read. But it does show that people have long noticed the strange relationship between reading and the voice.

Picture an old book open on a desk by lamplight, and a reader leaning over it in silence. Nothing moves except their eyes. And yet, somewhere inside, the words are becoming a story, with people and places and feelings. The question is whether a voice is doing that work, or something else.
In 2018, Russell Hurlburt's group turned their beepers on exactly this question.

Vincent Brouwers, Christopher Heavey, Russell Hurlburt and their colleagues published their study in the Journal of Consciousness Studies. Sixteen college students read short stories by F. Scott Fitzgerald and Ernest Hemingway, while a beeper sounded at random moments. At each beep, the students noted what was in their experience, and were interviewed carefully afterwards, just as in the earlier studies.

show.what: Beeped students reading short stories, and rarely found an inner voice narrating the text

segments.say: The result surprised many people. An inner voice narrating the text, saying the words of the story along with the eyes, showed up in only about three percent of the samples. The title of the paper said it plainly: silent reading is not silent speaking of the text.

show.title: Moments with inner narration of the text
show.label: of samples while reading stories (Brouwers et al., 2018)

segments.say: So what was going on instead? Inner pictures were frequent. People saw the scene, the room, the characters. Words did appear in roughly a quarter of the samples, but often not as a narration. Sometimes a reader was focused on one particular word from the text. Sometimes they were silently commenting on the story, in their own words. And sometimes the words had nothing to do with the book at all.

show.title: What readers did experience
items: Some words, about a quarter of samples
Their own comments on the story

segments.say: The authors suggested that one reason people overestimate the reading voice is that they expect it to be there. If you've always been told that reading is silent speech, then when you ask yourself whether you hear the words, you check, and in that moment of checking, you probably do. The act of looking may switch it on.
That doesn't mean the reading voice is a myth. Other studies suggest that, at least some of the time, our brains do bring voices into reading, especially when a text asks for it.

In 2008, Jessica Alexander and Lynne Nygaard at Emory University published a study about this. Participants first got to know two talkers, one who spoke quickly and one who spoke slowly. Later, they silently read passages that were said to have been written by one of them. The reading times suggested that people were, in a sense, hearing the writer's voice. They tended to read more slowly when the passage came from the slow talker, especially when the text was hard.

show.what: Readers seemed to read a text at the pace of the person they imagined saying it

segments.say: And in 2011, Bo Yao, Pascal Belin and Christoph Scheepers at the University of Glasgow published a brain imaging study in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. People silently read stories that contained either direct quotations, like, she said, I'm leaving, or indirect reports, like, she said that she was leaving. The direct quotations produced more activity in voice-sensitive areas of the auditory cortex.

show.who: Bo Yao, Pascal Belin & Christoph Scheepers
show.what: Reading quoted speech activated voice-sensitive parts of the brain more than reported speech

segments.say: So the picture is richer than either a yes or a no. Most of the time, readers probably don't narrate every word in their heads. Pictures and meaning often seem to lead. But voices can appear, especially when the text invites them, with a character speaking, or a writer whose voice you know. And, as always, people differ a great deal.

show.title: Putting it together
items: Voices appear when the text invites them

segments.say: If you'd like, you can try a small experiment the next time you read. Don't check constantly, because checking changes things. Just once or twice, stop suddenly and ask yourself, what was there, just then? A voice? A picture? A feeling? Nothing in particular? You might be surprised by what you find.

And whatever you find, it's fine. Some people hear every line of dialogue in a different voice, like a radio play. Some see a film. Some simply absorb the meaning, with very little inner sound at all. Each of these is a way of reading, and each of them gets the story from the page into the mind.
For our story tonight, reading offers one more lesson about the inner voice.

The inner voice may be less constant than we believe, even in the places where we're most certain it lives. And it seems to come and go depending on what the mind needs, appearing when a voice is useful, and stepping back when pictures or meaning can do the job better.

But when the voice does appear, where does it actually happen? Is it all in the brain, or does the body join in? A century ago, a few researchers tried to answer that by attaching sensors to the lips and throat of people who were only thinking.
